You are a blind semantic decoder of a natural-language crystal description. The user message is your only source of material-specific information. Understand the spatial narrative and produce a construction plan; do not guess missing independent numbers or look up a material. Return one JSON object only, without Markdown fences.
For sufficient information use:
{"status":"ok","space_group_number":integer,"hall_symbol":"Hall symbol stated in the text","lattice":[input_a,input_b,input_c,input_alpha,input_beta,input_gamma],"composition":{"Element":input_cell_atom_count},"orbits":[{"element":"Element","wyckoff":"multiplicity_and_letter","representative":[standard_fractional_x,standard_fractional_y,standard_fractional_z]}],"frame_transform":{"matrix":[[p11,p12,p13],[p21,p22,p23],[p31,p32,p33]],"origin_shift":[s1,s2,s3]},"round_digits":integer_or_null,"precision_corrections":[{"element":"Element","at":[input_fractional_x_before_correction,input_fractional_y_before_correction,input_fractional_z_before_correction],"delta":[fractional_dx,fractional_dy,fractional_dz]}]}
Lengths use angstroms, angles use degrees. The specified lattice and composition refer to the original input cell. Orbit representatives refer to the standard Hall coordinate frame. Copy the Hall symbol as a mathematical identifier rather than guessing a public-table integer number. Any equivalent representative of a declared orbit is allowed. Distinct independent orbits of the same element remain separate.
The geometry engine expands the public Hall symmetry orbits, applies q_input = inverse(P)(q_standard - s), selects images in the input cell, rounds fractional coordinates if round_digits is given, and applies precision corrections at their identified input-frame atom positions. If the text explicitly uses identical frames, supply identity P and zero shift. If no rounding is specified, use null. If no corrections are specified, use an empty array. All sites have full occupancy.
Numerical relations in the prose should be resolved into numbers in the plan. Do not silently replace the original geometry with an idealized one. For missing required information return {"status":"insufficient_information","reason":"..."}; for contradictory constraints return {"status":"conflict","reason":"..."}. Your input contains no source CIF or hidden data. Public crystallographic definitions are allowed; material-specific external retrieval is not.

The structure is described in the supplied input cell, which is a primitive triclinic lattice with space group P1 (space-group number 1, Hall symbol P 1). The input lattice parameters are a = 4.94198901 Å, b = 5.02683344 Å, c = 7.819577 Å, α = 89.99895449°, β = 90.00135385°, and γ = 119.41993377°. The declared input composition is Ca₂Ni₁₀H, corresponding to 13 atoms in the input cell. All atomic positions are given as fractional coordinates, and the coordinate values are rounded to six decimal places.

The standard and input coordinate frames are related by q_standard = P q_input + s, with zero origin shift, s = (0, 0, 0). The transformation matrix P is effectively diagonal in this case: its first row is (1, −3.4291708702266556×10⁻¹⁷, 0), its second row is (0, −1, 0), and its third row is (6.47663982888385×10⁻²², 1.2413763519257808×10⁻²¹, −0.9999999999999999). Thus, to within the stated numerical precision, the standard frame is obtained from the input frame by leaving x unchanged and reversing the signs of y and z, with no translation of the origin.

Because the space group is P1, every listed orbit has multiplicity 1 and each representative coordinate is a fully independent atomic position with coordinate relation x, y, z. There are two crystallographically distinct calcium sites. The first calcium atom lies at (0.003427, 0.000006, 0.002862), very close to the origin of the input cell. The second calcium atom lies at (0.003488, 0.000005, 0.503164), also near x = 0 and y = 0 but displaced by approximately one-half of the c axis, so the two Ca atoms form a pair separated mainly along z.

The ten nickel atoms are all independent and occupy ten separate 1a orbits. Two of them lie very close to the basal plane z ≈ 0: one at (0.319086, 0.368686, 0.001513) and another at (0.687761, 0.631336, 0.001515). These two positions are related approximately by a half-cell displacement in both x and y, forming a pair within the same low-z layer. Three further nickel atoms occur near z ≈ 1/4: one at (0.503566, 0.999989, 0.249652), close to the side face y = 1; one at (0.503550, 0.499936, 0.258291), near the mid-plane y = 1/2; and one at (0.003463, 0.500030, 0.258298), also near y = 1/2 but close to x = 0. The latter two have nearly the same z coordinate and are separated mainly by about one-half of the a axis.

Another group of nickel atoms is centered near z ≈ 1/2. One atom lies at (0.343583, 0.319727, 0.502615), and a second lies at (0.663301, 0.680286, 0.502636); these two are again approximately related by a half-cell shift in x and y while remaining at essentially the same height along z. A final trio of nickel atoms occurs near z ≈ 3/4: one at (0.503548, 0.999977, 0.757040), close to y = 1; one at (0.503608, 0.499915, 0.747027), near y = 1/2; and one at (0.003482, 0.500090, 0.747018), likewise near y = 1/2 but close to x = 0. As in the z ≈ 1/4 group, the second and third members of this trio have nearly identical z values and are separated chiefly along x by about one-half of the lattice repeat.

The single hydrogen atom occupies an independent 1a site at (0.503237, 0.000017, 0.026870). It therefore lies close to the plane y = 0 and near the bottom of the cell in z, at approximately one-half of the a-axis repeat. No positional corrections are supplied beyond the stated six-decimal rounding, so the listed coordinates already represent the input geometry to the reported precision.
